implementation_notes: Kotlin pushes immutability into the declaration: a val property cannot be reassigned, a data class with val constructor parameters generates equals, hashCode, toString and a copy() method that produces a modified instance, and the standard library separates the read-only List, Set and Map interfaces from their Mutable counterparts. Two gaps remain: the read-only interfaces are shallow, because the object behind them may still be a MutableList reached through an older reference, and copy() is shallow, so mutable components are shared with the copy. The hand-written form (explicit private backing field exposed as a read-only type) is still justified when the class is mutable internally but must publish an immutable face.
code_sketch:
data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

val p1 = Point(1, 2)
val p2 = p1.copy(y = 5)          // p1 is unchanged

fun total(items: List<Item>): Int = items.sumOf { it.price }  // read-only interface
pitfalls: A val reference to a MutableList is still mutable: listOf() returns a read-only interface, not an immutable implementation, and a caller holding the original MutableList changes what the value sees.
data class copy() is shallow: a MutableList component is shared between the original and the copy, so a mutation through one is visible in the other and in equals/hashCode.
Exposing a MutableList through a read-only type does not stop a downcast in Java interop; copy defensively or use persistent collections on API boundaries.

variants.name: kotlinx.collections.immutable persistent collections
variants.implementation_notes: When a model is updated often enough that copying whole collections hurts, kotlinx.collections.immutable supplies persistent List, Set and Map implementations whose modification operations return new instances sharing the unchanged structure, plus builders and a mutate { } helper that batches changes and freezes the result. They implement the read-only interfaces (ImmutableList extends List), so call sites keep their signatures while the immutability guarantee becomes real rather than conventional.
variants.code_sketch:
val base: PersistentList<Int> = persistentListOf(1, 2, 3)
val next = base.add(4)                                  // base is untouched
val built = base.mutate { it.add(5); it.removeAt(0) }   // batch, then freeze
pitfalls: Persistent collections still hold references to their elements: if an element is mutable, the collection's value can change through that element.
persistentListOf/persistentMapOf are not drop-in replacements for listOf/mapOf: persistent updates are O(log n) and iteration is slower than ArrayList, so use them where updates and sharing dominate.
